lesson.title: From Chance to Numbers: What Makes a Random Variable Discrete
lesson.summary: A random variable turns the outcome of a chance process into a number, and it is discrete when its possible values can be listed or counted rather than measured on a continuous scale.
lesson.body:
A random variable is simply a rule that assigns a numerical value to every outcome of a chance process. Once you can attach a number to what happens, you can start asking questions using the tools of algebra and arithmetic instead of just describing outcomes in words. Random variables come in two basic types, discrete and continuous, and the difference matters because it determines which formulas and techniques apply to a given problem.

A discrete random variable is one whose possible values form a list you could, in principle, write out one at a time, even if the list happens to be long. There are gaps between consecutive values, and nothing can fall in between them. Think about X, the number of pets owned by a randomly chosen student at a school. If the data show no student owns more than 3 pets, then X can only take the values 0, 1, 2, or 3. A student cannot own 1.5 pets or 2.7 pets, so every possible outcome lands on one of these four whole numbers with nothing in between.

This is exactly what discrete means as a variable type: countable, separated values, the kind you could list on your fingers. A continuous random variable, by contrast, can take any value in an interval of real numbers. If instead you measured Y, the exact weight in pounds of a student's dog, Y could be 12.0, 12.03, 12.031, or any value in between, limited only by the precision of your scale. There is no smallest gap between possible weights the way there is between 1 pet and 2 pets. That is why weight, height, and time are continuous, while counts like number of pets, number of siblings, or number of heads in a series of coin flips are discrete.

The distinction is not just a vocabulary exercise. Discrete random variables are described using probabilities attached to individual values, something like there is a 40 percent chance a randomly chosen student owns exactly 1 pet. Continuous random variables need a different approach, since the chance of hitting any single exact value is essentially zero, and probabilities are instead assigned to intervals. Everything in the chapters that follow, expected value, variance, standard deviation, sums and differences, is built on the discrete case, where you can list every value and attach a probability to each one directly.

To make X, the number of pets, fully useful, you need more than just the list of possible values 0, 1, 2, and 3. You need to know how likely each value is. Suppose that among all students at the school, 20 percent own 0 pets, 40 percent own 1 pet, 30 percent own 2 pets, and 10 percent own 3 pets. That complete pairing of values with probabilities is called a probability distribution, and it is the subject of the next chapter. For now, the key idea to hold onto is this: a discrete random variable is defined by its countable list of possible values, and everything statistics lets you do with it, finding an average outcome, measuring how spread out the results are, starts from that list.
